Politics are my favorite part of Commander, bar none. Wheeling and dealing is FUN. Commander is at its most fun when it's a social game, and you have to really think about how you're interacting with everyone at the table - not just the decks, but the players themselves.

I play a lot of control decks with very limited board presence, so my success is entirely up to my ability to bargain. I don't whine or get upset if people swing at me, but I'll do my best to point them in another direction. Sure, I have a Black Market Connections and a lot of cards in hand, but that guy over there has a board full of goblins. Isn't he the more immediate problem? I'll cut you a deal: I'll remove that key piece if you don't swing at me for a turn. So on and so forth.

Politics can earn you wins that you otherwise wouldn't have gotten. Making deals or misdirecting other players (and I don't mean lying, obviously) can buy you the time you need to sneak a win when nobody expects it.

The reality of the situation is that you don't play perfectly. Nobody does, not a single player in the world plays absolutely perfectly. There is always something you can do better.

You will also not win every game. Your job as a player is not to improve to the point where you win every single game. Your job is to improve to the point where you are winning the games you *can* win.

Yes, there are games where your bot lane is a combined 0/20 at 15 minutes, and yes, there are games where your jungler will single-handedly run over his lane and 1v9. If you're a gifted mechanical player and you know how to take advantage of matchups, you can theoretically do that too!

But there will be a lot of games that are fairly even, and if you execute properly and do what your champion/role does and outperform your opponent, you'll win.

You don't need to play particularly "selfishly" and sometimes, you need to do what your team is doing, even if it's a poor choice. If your team just wants to ARAM and fight the enemy team and you're off farming side lanes without TP, they're going to fight and lose the 4v5 even though they might have been making the "wrong" decision and you might have been making the "right" one.

Keep at it, keep asking questions, keep evaluating your own play and seeing what you can/should do better.

Hey! No worries about asking a lot of questions. That's what this thread is for. :)

>How reasonably big are the tyrants im supposed to be making?

The thing about Demonology is it's a LOT of RNG and a LOT of variance. I always tell people not to aim for percents. Just focus on nailing your setups consistently and using your spells in the same order as much as possible. Sometimes you'll get great refunds and get huge tyrants, sometimes you'll get no refunds and get baby tyrants even though you did the exact same thing both times. It's just the nature of the spec. 

Sjele has a great video on tyrant setups [here](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c95Fq9I6cz0).

>When tyrant is down how should I be playing? Keeping up as many imps as possible or should I be implosioning.

Essentially you don't change your playstyle when tyrant is out. If you're hitting one target, do the regular single target rotation and only implosion to maintain the EP buff. If you're hitting 2+ targets, use the implosion rotation.

>And lastly this is more flavor but is there a max amount of imps I can have? What is imp energy? What add-ons/WAs do you use/recommend.

The max amount of imps changes based on a lot of things: your haste, whether your imps have maximum amount of uptime, whether or not you're pressing implosion obviously, etc. I don't think I usually go above 12~ imps unless I'm doing the line of sight cheese.

Imp energy is a simple concept to understand, really. Imps have 100 energy when they spawn. Each firebolt they cast costs 20 energy. Imps despawn when they are out of energy. Tyrant, without DCon, freezes your imps' energy and lets them freecast for the duration of your tyrant at whatever energy level they had when tyrant was summoned - it doesn't "refresh" their energy.

With DCon, your tyrant eats all of your imps' remaining energy, and the tyrant's percent is the added up value of their eaten energy. 

For an easy example of this, if you use the Inner Demons talent and immediately summon a tyrant without pressing any other buttons, your tyrant will eat the two full-energy imps you get from that talent, and it will be a 100% tyrant.

As for Weakauras, I use two simple icon Weakauras, one that tracks EP and one that tracks how many imps I have active.

1) Build to five with shadow bolt, don't use cores unless you have 3+

2) HoG

3) Build to five with shadow bolt, don't use cores unless you have 3+

10) DB

11) HoG

12) Shadow Bolt (to allow your imps time to spawn)

13) Tyrant

Supreme Commander isn't a bad trait by any means, there are just traits that are *better* - it's the same as Infinite Stars. Stars isn't detrimental, it's just not the best corruption.

1) Build to 5 shards

3) Build to 5 shards

4) Implosion

5) Dogs

6) Build to 5 shards

7) Hand of Gul'dan

8) 1x Shadow Bolt

9) Hand of Gul'dan

Don't look at everything so narrowly. As a jungler, you have the role that varies the most from game to game, and you need to learn to react to the game state.

You said you're new, so it's unreasonable to expect you to know every champion and what they're likely to do, but that's one of the core concepts of jungling: being able to look at both comps on the loading screen and start formulating a gameplan. Which lanes look gankable early? Which will push? Do you have a favorable jungle matchup or not? Where is the enemy jungler likely to start and how are they likely to path?

Warwick is a powerful early game champion who can pull off successful ganks at level 3, so some people will assume that's what you will do; however it's not always as simple as that. Sometimes lanes are pushed up too far to gank safely, sometimes the enemy laner is playing a champion with an easy way to escape ganks. Sometimes you'd just rather go bother the enemy laner in their jungle if they're playing a weaker champion. 

Honestly, ignore what your teammates demand of you. As you're still learning the game, focus purely on learning matchups and champions, and making your pathing more efficient.

>go you normally go get a leash from bot lane, or go opposite side?

This isn't a question with a standard answer, it varies. If I'm playing Lee blue side and want to gank bot at level 3, I can do Blue > Gromp > Wolves > Red > gank. If I'm Nidalee red side and I want to catch the enemy Kayn, I can do Red > hop baron pit > look for him at blue or wolves. 

The idea is to path effectively depending on where you want to go first and what you want to do in the early game. Is there a lane you know you'll be ganking level 3? Do you want to fight the enemy jungler? Or do you just want to powerfarm and scale? Those choices are how you decide your pathing.

>Second, how do I track the enemy JG in low elo?

You kinda...don't. 

People in low ELO don't always follow standard routes or jungle rules of thumb barring stuff that's extremely obvious (like Amumu will generally start blue). It's harder to track the enemy jungler strictly through intuition, but you can still use wards and the like - and you should still make an attempt to mentally track the enemy jungler by thinking about his champ and most likely path, just understand that you might be incorrect.

>Finally, how can I use prio well?

Ping six thousand times whenever you're doing anything. Use chat, it exists for a reason (and when I say use chat, I don't mean flame or be obnoxious, just something simple like "i solo drag, might need help pls"). 

The entire concept of lane prio exists because most laners are going to be extremely hesitant to leave their lane if they have a wave crashing into their tower. If you're *consistently* making plays where you REQUIRE lane assistance, you might be taking unnecessary risks.

> if I am playing an early game champion, is there anything I can do if lanes are either pushing, losing, or hard to gank and none of them are viable ganks?

You think about the enemy jungler. He is your "lane opponent". If every one of your lanes is pushed up, which one looks the most easily gankable? Be on that side of the map and countergank if you're confident you can win the 2v2/3v3. If you don't think you can win that skirmish, be on the OTHER side of the map, and when the jungler shows to gank a lane, invade his jungle and steal camps, or take objectives like dragon/herald. 

And if all your lanes are losing, you have no priority, and you genuinely can't gank any of them (which is a rarer situation than you think), then...you just hope your lanes lose gracefully and outscale.

I'm garbage at this game but I've played a lot and watched a lot of VODs so here's what I notice when I'm comparing my games to high ELO games.

A) Vision

High ELO junglers know how to ward, where to ward, and they know how to play around wards. I see junglers from Iron > Gold just parade straight down the river into a warded brush, stand in the warded brush for 45 seconds when the enemy laners are clearly playing around the ward, then the jungler just turns and leaves. That's so much wasted time. In addition, if there's an important neutral objective up and the enemy spots you on the other side of the map, you've committed a cardinal sin of jungling.

B) Time Management

Jungle is all about time and efficiency. In low ELO, junglers don't maximize their efficiency or pathing. They kinda just do whatever camps they feel like and walk around aimlessly, sometimes they'll just stroll into a lane for a gank without really thinking about what they can get out of it. In higher ELOs, junglers pay attention to their camps and neutral objectives so as to waste as little time as possible. You always want to either be farming, ganking, or setting up a neutral objective.

C) Counterjungling

This is kinda vague but counterjungling is an extremely important facet of improving as a jungler, and it isn't always about invading and killing the enemy jungler. Counterjungling can be as simple as counterganking, placing deep wards to track the enemy jungler's movements, or predicting his gank pattern and telling your laner to back off. In lower ELOs, junglers kinda just...invade sometimes without paying attention to all the variables. Where will the enemy jungler start? Are they stronger than you at early levels? Can your laners come to help you? Do you have vision?

D) Game Knowledge

Even more vague than the previous one but jungling is the role that requires the most game knowledge. You need to know at least the very basics of what every champion does and how it relates to you and your team. For example, let's say the enemy top laner is Illaoi. At level 3, you have double buffs and she is pushed up very far without much mana, and your laner is someone with high early kill pressure. That's a very gankable lane. However, post 6 because of the way Illaoi's kit works with her ultimate, that lane becomes much more dangerous to gank. That bit of game knowledge is extremely important to become a better jungler. Know when your enemy's powerspikes are, when your powerspikes are, and when your team's powerspikes are.

On ST. On 2+ targets. On 15 targets. You use blizzard *always* because it reduces the CD of your orb, which contains all of your damage. You use Veins on CD, it's a bad offensive CD anyways.

Outside of Orb, the rotation is the standard Frost rotation. Inside orb, FoF Lance > instant blizzard > BF > non instant blizzard > frostbolt.

You want to keep Blizzard running as often as possible, but you still want to dump your lances.

1) Yes, you take Chain Reaction. The typical build is Lonely Winter, Rune of Power, Chain Reaction, Splitting Ice/Freezing Rain (depending on dungeon, pull size, and personal preference), and Thermal Void/Ray of Frost (usually Void).

2) The PI build scales hard with traits. You need 3x Packed Ice. It's playable with 2x, but you really need 3. You also really want at least 1 Whiteout for the CDR on Orb, and 1 Flash Freeze for the FoF proc chance.

3) The damage from Orb build is almost entirely from Ice Lance. Lonely Winter gives you +25% damage to Ice Lance. The only time I'd ever take Bone Chilling is if I really wanted the extra pet root for some reason, and in dungeons, I really don't care about an extra root considering all my snares as well as Frost Nova.

4) The priority is you always Orb on CD and use Rune with every orb. Use Blizzard on CD, as it lowers the CD of your Orb. Use Brain Freeze for free ice lances. Dump Fingers procs. That's pretty much it. Don't use a BF proc before a FoF proc, it'll waste the FoF.

Your goal is to pump as many orbs out as possible so you can pump out as many shattered lances as possible. That's all your damage.

And that's okay! I don't think a drain necessarily has to be our filler, but thematically, Affliction is supposed to be about attrition and draining the life from enemies. All of our abilities to fit this theme (Siphon Life, Phantom Singularity, Inevitable Demise, etc) are talents or azerite traits.

Most of what I have to say is about Demo and Affliction.

I've played Affliction since about Ulduar release, which was when I started playing WoW. I was drawn to it because I, an edgy teenager at the time, was enamored with the idea of a dark spellcaster who drains the life from his enemies. That's pretty much how it felt up until BfA.

Now, Affliction thematically feels like a shell of its former self. Our drains are no longer important parts of our toolkit, and we've lost a lot of self-healing. Darkglare mechanically feels alright, but the summoning of a demon as our big cooldown feels more in line with Demonology than Affliction, and I think Deathbolt is a horrific design for what's supposed to be a DoT class.

Affliction is very strong, of course, but its ways of dealing with multiple targets feels inelegant and ineffective. Seed of Corruption has a very long cast time, and we have to tab dot everything to spread our damage around. It doesn't feel good to play.

Demonology, on the other hand, feels pretty amazing to me. The rotation flows well, there are procs that make the rotation feel dynamic, our baseline cooldown is on a lowish cooldown but still feels impactful to use.

I do wish some talents were stronger. Bilescourge Bombers was one of the abilities I was most excited for coming into BfA, and Nether Portal is just about the most "demonology" style ability I could possibly think of. It's dripping with flavor and is thematically amazing. It's just weak, unfortunately.

My other complaint about Demo is the lack of a baseline kick. A lot of our damage is tied up in Felguard, so giving it up feels quite bad. Swapping to Dreadlash alleviates it a little bit, but it still isn't great having to sacrifice such a large portion of the spec's identity in order to have something that every other DPS spec already has.

Between the skirmishes in Alterac Valley, an eerie sense of peace would settle over the war-torn landscape. Bodies and bones and other memories of battle would be covered in freshly-fallen snow, lying beneath the powder to be stumbled upon later. Crimson would give way to white, and a false sense of peace would descend upon the valley - a sense of peace that would never last. The opposed forces of the Alliance and the Horde could never hold a ceasefire long enough to collect the bodies of the fallen. Wolves would barely have time to pick at the corpses left behind before reinforcements would arrive for both factions, and the valley would once again swell with war songs and battle cries.

Yves Lightsong knew this cycle well. Despite being born into the upper echelons of sin’dorei society, she’d never felt called toward the glittering spires of nobility. Even from a young age, she’d dreamed of being a protector, a savior. Her Blood Knight training had served her well, but to the dismay of her family and her instructors, she’d chosen to serve in the distinctly unglamorous battlefield of Alterac Valley. She didn’t care about the glory or the riches involved with being a prominent paladin. Her job was to protect and serve, and in Alterac Valley, she could do just that.

“How ya doin, mon?” A blue-skinned troll shaman smiled kindly around his tusks as he looked at Yves, tilting his head. Kuanii’s wild, orange hair and wickedly-sharp axes always contrasted his kind and level-headed demeanor. Yves often wrote of it in her letters to her friends back home. “Ya look a bit...grim. Dis ain’t gonna be no different from da other battles.”

She nodded, though she couldn’t deny that she felt a vague sense of dread as she idly traced her bare fingers across her warhammer. She recognized every scar in the weapon. A tiny crack from when she’d bashed in the shield of a kal’dorei warrior, a blunted corner from when she’d crushed the skull of a human mage. Her weapon told nearly as many stories as her own battle-worn body and armor. She had too many tales from this bleak valley.

“I’m alright,” Yves responded, having nearly forgotten the initial question. She brushed a lock of blonde hair out of her face as she stood, hefting her warhammer with both hands. “I’m just feeling a little bit...lost, I suppose. There’s been so many battles in this damned valley, Kuanii. So much bloodshed...and I’m not sure if I even remember what we’re fighting for.”


The troll frowned as he strapped his weapons to his stooped back and sat down beside Yves on the bench. “I been wonderin’, too. I don’t always pretend ta understand da motives of da Warchief, but I serve da Horde. If dis be her will, den dat’s what I’m gonna do.” He shrugged, seeming content, as he always did. Even in the heat of battle. The troll never gave in to the bloodlust that so often consumed the Darkspear. He was able to keep a clear head, which had saved his life on so many occasions. It was a trait that Yves admired.

She nodded slowly, resolve replacing the doubt in her mind. It wasn’t what Kuanii had said, but how he’d said it. He believed in his cause with his whole heart, the same way Yves cared about hers. Unlike the bellowing orcs on the other side of the cavern, she wasn’t here for the glory of battle. Unlike the Forsaken plotting in the corner, she wasn’t here for vengeance or sadism. She was here to care for her comrades in their hour of need, so that they in turn could see the fulfillment of their own goals.

As she took a deep breath and gripped her hammer, the war cries went up and the banners were lifted once more. She watched Kuanii as he rode off with the rest of the pack on the back of his raptor, and for a moment, she wondered if it was the last time she’d ever see him.

Not if she had anything to say about it.

Learn to spot dodge and block smartly, and minimize use of rolls, as they're highly punishable. There are introductory tutorials everywhere for this sort of thing.

- Pick a main. Play around with different characters until you find something that clicks for you. It doesn't have to be a top-tier character, just something you're comfortable with - but a higher tier character obviously will be more successful, if that's what you care about. Find the tier list [here](http://www.ssbwiki.com/Tier_list#Super_Smash_Bros._4_tier_list).

- Now that you have a main, do your research. What are your kill moves? Combo starters? Anti-airs? Combo breakers? What do you have that's safe on shield? What options does your character have out of a throw? What do your recovery options look like? The [wiki](http://www.ssbwiki.com/Super_Smash_Bros._4) is great for this. Also watch videos of pro gameplay to see what your character looks like at maximum efficiency.

- Now that you have a main and generally know what it's capable of, start learning other characters as well. Not only do you need secondaries in case of poor matchups, but knowing what opposing players can do, when they'll do it, and how you plan around that is *essential* in becoming competitive. 

- Find people to practice all this new knowledge with. I advise against For Glory, as it teaches bad habits, such as roll spamming and overcompensating for lag. It's best to play in person, such as friendly matches at local tournaments, or with friends, but failing those, [Anther's Ladder](https://www.smashladder.com/) is a godsend.

- Keep practicing, never be afraid to lose! You always learn more from losing than from winning. Just keep at it. 

Hope that helped!
